\section{Engines and Learning}\label{sec:engines}

CGT predicts which endgames are hard for an engine: an infinitesimal such as ${\uparrow}$ is a fight over one
spare tempo and a nimber such as $\star$ a fight over parity, and neither shows in the material, so a static
evaluation misses them until the search reaches the end of the fight.

\subsection{A CGT Test Suite}

We built $233$ legal positions on the ordinary $8\times8$ board with at most seven men, each labeled by the class of its CGT value
(Table~\ref{tab:sf}). In $181$ of them the Lichess tablebase~\cite{LichessTB} confirms the winning moves that
CGT predicts; in the other $52$ the model and the tablebase disagree, so we score the engines against the
tablebase.

\subsection{Stockfish and Lc0}

We ran Stockfish~19~\cite{Stockfish} on one thread with a $64$~MB hash and no tablebases. It solves all $233$
positions at $10^5$ nodes, and $232$ already at $10^3$ \lab{C1}. The classes separate at a small fixed depth
(Table~\ref{tab:sf}). At depth~1 the engine reads hot positions, numbers and switches correctly
$73$--$81\%$ of the time, but infinitesimals only $30\%$ ($26\%$ at depth~2) and nimbers $53\%$
\lab{C1}: exactly the tempo and parity fights that CGT singles out. Both classes reach $100\%$ by depth~8.
With one engine and a small sample, this is a pilot result.

Lc0~v0.32.1~\cite{Lc0}, with its bundled network, is perfect at all four budgets, $10^3$ to $10^6$ nodes:
every best move keeps the tablebase result and every evaluation matches it, and it calls all $17$ draws
correctly from $10^3$ nodes on \lab{C1}. At practical budgets the suite is therefore too easy for both
engines; only Stockfish at small fixed depth separates the classes.

\subsection{ChessSums}

Beyond seven men no tablebase applies, but CGT still values sums exactly. We built ChessSums, a set of
$26{,}000$ pawn-endgame sums whose components come from a library of $418$ with $37$ distinct values; every
component has the same value in all nine settings (Section~\ref{sec:ep}). Whole-board alpha--beta confirms every outcome
except five that hit its time limit \lab{C1}, and an independent minimax confirms $4{,}887$ of them
\lab{C2}. Alpha--beta, blind to the split,
needs about $4$--$9$ times as many nodes per added component \lab{C1}, while adding the CGT values costs
almost nothing.

\subsection{Engines on Sums}

We placed each sum on the ordinary $8\times8$ board beside T (Fig.~\ref{fig:trebuchet}) or a shifted copy that our
king-and-pawn solver confirms is a mutual zugzwang, giving legal positions with $15$--$20$ men. On $200$ of
them, Stockfish~19 picks a move in the winning set only $26.5$--$28.0\%$ of the time from $10^3$ to $10^6$
nodes, and Lc0 $32.5$--$33.5\%$ at $10^3$ and $10^4$ nodes \lab{C1} ($45$ of the $200$ are second-player
wins with no winning move; excluding them, $34$--$36\%$ and $42$--$43\%$). More nodes barely help, both engines get
worse as components are added, and the errors do not single out nimbers or infinitesimals.

The ground truth here is the model with frozen kings, which is not always exact
(Section~\ref{sec:kings-sweep}), so these numbers measure agreement with the model, not real-chess errors.

\subsection{Learning Dawson's Chess}

Can a network learn CGT? In normal-play Dawson's chess (Section~\ref{sec:dawson}) the first player wins exactly
when the strips' Grundy values have a nonzero nim-sum~\cite{GuySmith1956,WinningWays}. An LSTM value network
in PyTorch~\cite{PyTorch}, trained on total lengths up to $30$, reaches $0.82$ test accuracy on total lengths
$31$--$80$, against about $0.79$ for the majority guess \lab{C1}. The rule itself scores $1.0$, so the network has not
learned it, and linear probes on its strip embedding do no better than the majority guess.
